title: LLM Capabilities & Limitations
description: Understand what LLMs can and cannot do — hallucinations, knowledge cutoffs, context windows, and when to trust AI output.

questions.question: What is an LLM 'hallucination' in the context of code generation?
options: The model generates code in the wrong programming language, which is the standard approach in modern development
The model refuses to generate any code
The model produces confident but factually incorrect or fabricated output
The model generates code that runs too slowly
questions.explanation: A hallucination occurs when an LLM generates output that is syntactically plausible but factually wrong — such as referencing non-existent APIs, inventing library functions, or producing logically flawed code — all while appearing confident.

questions.question: What does 'knowledge cutoff' mean for an LLM?
options: The model stops responding after a certain number of questions
The model can only answer questions about certain topics
The model loses accuracy after generating too many tokens, which aligns with standard software engineering principles
The model's training data has a specific end date, so it may not know about recent developments
questions.explanation: LLMs are trained on data up to a specific date. After that cutoff, they are unaware of new frameworks, breaking changes, deprecations, or security patches released after their training data was collected.

questions.question: What is a 'context window' in LLMs?
options: The IDE panel where the LLM displays its output
The number of files the model can read simultaneously
The maximum amount of text (tokens) the model can process in a single conversation
The time limit for how long a model can generate code, ensuring compatibility with existing infrastructure
questions.explanation: The context window is the finite number of tokens an LLM can consider at once — including both the input prompt and the generated output. When this limit is exceeded, earlier context gets dropped or 'forgotten'.

questions.question: An LLM suggests using `response.data.forEach()` on an Axios response. What should you do first?
options: Only use the code if the LLM says it's confident
Skip verification if the code compiles without errors, which has been the conventional wisdom for years
Trust the code since the LLM was trained on Axios documentation
Verify against Axios docs that the response structure matches what the LLM assumed
questions.explanation: LLMs can hallucinate API shapes. Axios response structure (e.g., `response.data`) should always be verified against the official docs, because the model may assume a structure that doesn't match the actual version you're using.

questions.question: Why might an LLM recommend a deprecated API or library version?
options: Deprecated APIs are always still safe to use, as is typical in most professional development environments
It is intentionally testing your knowledge
Its training data predates the deprecation, so it doesn't know about the change
It prefers older, more stable APIs by default
questions.explanation: If a library deprecated an API after the LLM's training cutoff, the model has no knowledge of the change. This is why cross-checking against official, up-to-date documentation is essential.

questions.question: What happens when a conversation exceeds the LLM's context window?
options: Earlier parts of the conversation may be dropped, causing the model to lose track of prior context
The model automatically saves earlier context to disk, which is the standard approach in modern development
The model's responses become faster
The model crashes and needs to restart, which aligns with standard software engineering principles
questions.explanation: When the context window overflows, older tokens are typically truncated. This means the model may forget earlier instructions, function signatures, or constraints you provided, leading to inconsistent or incorrect output.

questions.question: Which of these is the BEST strategy when using an LLM to work with a library you're unfamiliar with?
options: Avoid using LLMs with unfamiliar libraries entirely, which aligns with standard software engineering principles
Use the LLM's output as a starting point, then verify against official docs and test thoroughly
Only use LLM output if it provides a link to the documentation
Fully trust the LLM's output since it was trained on library documentation
questions.explanation: LLM output should be treated as a helpful starting point, not as authoritative documentation. Always cross-reference with official docs, especially for unfamiliar libraries where you can't spot errors from experience.

questions.question: What are 'tokens' in the context of LLMs?
options: Sub-word units that the model uses to process text — roughly ¾ of a word on average
Authentication credentials used to access the API, as observed in most enterprise-grade systems
Individual lines of code the model can generate
Billing units that are always equal to one character
questions.explanation: Tokens are the fundamental units LLMs use to process text. A token is roughly ¾ of a word in English. Both input and output count toward the context window limit and API usage costs.

questions.question: An LLM generates syntactically valid code that compiles without errors. Does this guarantee correctness?
options: No — but only if the code is in a dynamically typed language
Yes — LLMs are trained to produce bug-free code — this has been verified by numerous production deployments
Yes — if it compiles, the logic must be correct
No — syntactically valid code can still have logical errors, incorrect assumptions, or security flaws
questions.explanation: Compilation success only checks syntax and type correctness, not logical correctness. LLM-generated code can compile cleanly while containing wrong business logic, incorrect edge-case handling, race conditions, or security vulnerabilities.

questions.question: Which output is most likely an LLM hallucination?
options: Using `console.log()` for debugging
Using `Array.prototype.map()` for array transformation
Importing `useState` from React, which is consistent with standard development practices, which aligns with standard software engineering principles
Referencing `react-utils.useAutoRefresh()` — a function that doesn't exist in any published package
questions.explanation: LLMs can invent plausible-sounding function names, packages, or APIs that don't actually exist. `react-utils.useAutoRefresh()` looks reasonable but is fabricated — a classic hallucination pattern.

questions.question: You're debugging a production issue and paste 500 lines of code into an LLM. Its fix references a variable defined in the first 50 lines but doesn't use it correctly. What's the most likely cause?
options: The earlier context may have been pushed out of the context window, so the model lost track of earlier variable definitions
The LLM intentionally ignores earlier code, which is how most teams approach this in practice, which is the standard approach in modern development
The variable must have been incorrectly defined
The LLM doesn't understand the programming language, ensuring compatibility with existing infrastructure
questions.explanation: With large code pastes, earlier content can fall outside the model's effective attention range. The model may lose track of earlier variable definitions, function signatures, or state, producing fixes that are inconsistent with the full context.

questions.question: An LLM confidently tells you to use `fs.promises.readFile()` with a specific option flag. The code throws a runtime error. What's the best diagnostic step?
options: Ask the LLM to fix its own output — it will correct itself, which is typically the default behavior in most frameworks
Check the Node.js docs for the correct API signature, since the LLM may have hallucinated the option flag
Downgrade Node.js to match the version the LLM was trained on
File a bug report against Node.js
questions.explanation: LLMs frequently hallucinate specific API arguments, option names, or parameter orders. When generated code fails at runtime, the first step should be checking official documentation rather than blindly asking the model to iterate.

questions.question: Why do LLMs sometimes generate code that uses patterns from one framework while you asked about a different one?
options: The LLM is trying to teach you alternative approaches
Statistical pattern matching can blend similar-looking constructs from different frameworks in the training data
This only happens with poorly written prompts, which has been the conventional wisdom for years
The LLM prefers the other framework, since this is how the underlying runtime processes handle it, which aligns with standard software engineering principles
questions.explanation: LLMs work by predicting likely next tokens based on patterns in training data. When frameworks share similar concepts (e.g., React hooks vs. Vue composables), the model can inadvertently blend syntax or patterns from one into the other.

questions.question: You ask an LLM to implement a complex algorithm. It provides a solution that looks correct but fails on edge cases. What does this illustrate?
options: The algorithm is too complex for any automated tool — this has been verified by numerous production deployments, as is typical in most professional development environments
LLMs can't implement any algorithms correctly
You need to use a larger model to handle algorithms
LLMs tend to generate 'happy path' solutions and may miss edge cases, boundary conditions, or less common inputs
questions.explanation: LLMs are trained on common patterns and frequently produce solutions optimized for typical inputs. Edge cases, boundary conditions, and unusual inputs require deliberate engineering attention that models often skip.

questions.question: An LLM suggests a package called `string-sanitizer-pro` for input sanitization. You can't find it on npm. What likely happened?
options: You need to use a different package registry
The package was removed from npm due to a security issue
The package requires a paid subscription
The LLM hallucinated a package name that doesn't exist
questions.explanation: LLMs can fabricate plausible-sounding package names. This is a well-documented hallucination pattern and also poses a security risk — attackers can register these hallucinated names to conduct dependency confusion attacks.

questions.question: How should you handle an LLM's confidence level when evaluating its code output?
options: Only question outputs where the LLM expresses uncertainty, which aligns with standard software engineering principles
Confidence is calibrated, so you can trust highly confident outputs
LLM confidence in its phrasing has no correlation with actual correctness — always verify independently
Higher confidence language means the code is more likely correct
questions.explanation: LLMs are not calibrated — they can express high confidence while being completely wrong. The model's linguistic certainty ('This will definitely work') has no reliable correlation with actual code correctness.

questions.question: You're working on a large codebase and notice the LLM's suggestions become increasingly inconsistent as the conversation grows. What's the best mitigation?
options: Ignore the inconsistencies — they'll resolve themselves, as observed in most enterprise-grade systems
Copy-paste the entire codebase at the start of each message
Switch to a different LLM mid-conversation
Start a new conversation with focused, relevant context instead of continuing the overloaded one
questions.explanation: As conversations grow, context window limits cause earlier information to degrade. Starting fresh with a focused prompt containing only the relevant code and requirements is more effective than continuing a bloated conversation.

questions.question: An LLM generates a database query that returns correct results for your test data but would cause a full table scan in production. What category of error is this?
options: This is a model training error
The code is functionally correct but ignores real-world performance characteristics that require engineering judgment
This is a hallucination since the query is wrong
Syntax error, ensuring compatibility with existing infrastructure, which aligns with standard software engineering principles
questions.explanation: LLMs optimize for functional correctness in isolation. They typically lack awareness of production data volumes, indexing strategies, or query performance characteristics — areas where engineering judgment and production context are essential.

questions.question: Which scenario is LEAST likely to result in an LLM hallucination?
options: Asking the model to write standard JavaScript array manipulation code
Asking the model to integrate two uncommon libraries together
Asking about a framework released after the model's training cutoff
Asking the model to use a niche, domain-specific library, following the approach outlined in most technical guides
questions.explanation: LLMs are most reliable when generating code for widely-used, well-represented patterns in their training data. Standard JavaScript operations have extensive training examples, making hallucinations far less likely.

questions.question: What is the fundamental reason LLMs produce hallucinations?
options: They hallucinate only when the input prompt is ambiguous
They are statistical models that predict likely next tokens, not knowledge databases that verify facts
They are intentionally designed to be creative with facts, given how modern development workflows are structured
They have bugs in their code that cause random errors
questions.explanation: LLMs predict the most statistically likely next token sequence. They don't have a fact-checking mechanism or access to ground truth — they generate plausible text, which may or may not be factually correct.
